claim: N6-methyladenine (6mA) DNA modification has recently been described in metazoans, including in Drosophila.
source: N6-methyladenine (6mA) DNA modification has recently been described in metazoans, including in Drosophila, for which the erasure of this epigenetic mark has been ascribed to the ten-eleven translocation (TET) enzyme.
evidence: The claim is supported by references to prior literature describing 6mA in metazoans and Drosophila.

claim: The erasure of 6mA in Drosophila has been ascribed to the ten-eleven translocation (TET) enzyme.
source: N6-methyladenine (6mA) DNA modification has recently been described in metazoans, including in Drosophila, for which the erasure of this epigenetic mark has been ascribed to the ten-eleven translocation (TET) enzyme.
evidence: The claim references prior attribution of 6mA erasure to TET in Drosophila.

claim: Traces of 6mA were found by LC-MS/MS in Drosophila under axenic or conventional breeding conditions.
source: Using axenic or conventional breeding conditions, we found traces of 6mA by LC-MS/MS and no significant increase in 6mA levels in the absence of TET, suggesting that this modification is present at very low levels in the Drosophila genome but not regulated by TET.
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is no significant increase in 6mA levels in the absence of TET in Drosophila.
source: Using axenic or conventional breeding conditions, we found traces of 6mA by LC-MS/MS and no significant increase in 6mA levels in the absence of TET, suggesting that this modification is present at very low levels in the Drosophila genome but not regulated by TET.
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data comparing wild-type and TET mutant samples.

claim: 6mA is present at very low levels in the Drosophila genome.
source: Using axenic or conventional breeding conditions, we found traces of 6mA by LC-MS/MS and no significant increase in 6mA levels in the absence of TET, suggesting that this modification is present at very low levels in the Drosophila genome but not regulated by TET.
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS measurements showing very low 6mA levels.

claim: 6mA is not regulated by TET in Drosophila.
source: Using axenic or conventional breeding conditions, we found traces of 6mA by LC-MS/MS and no significant increase in 6mA levels in the absence of TET, suggesting that this modification is present at very low levels in the Drosophila genome but not regulated by TET.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of 6mA increase in TET mutants.

claim: TET does not demethylate 6mA in Drosophila.
source: Consistent with this latter hypothesis, further molecular and genetic analyses showed that TET does not demethylate 6mA but acts essentially in an enzymatic-independent manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular and genetic analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: TET acts essentially in an enzymatic-independent manner in Drosophila.
source: Consistent with this latter hypothesis, further molecular and genetic analyses showed that TET does not demethylate 6mA but acts essentially in an enzymatic-independent manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic analyses using catalytic-dead TET mutants.

claim: TET non-enzymatic activity is important for fly development.
source: Our results call for further caution concerning the role and regulation of 6mA DNA modification in metazoans and underline the importance of TET non-enzymatic activity for fly development.
evidence: The claim is supported by viability and developmental analyses of catalytic-dead TET mutants.

claim: 6mA was considered to be essentially restricted to the genome of prokaryotes until recently.
source: Until recently, N6-methyl-2'-deoxyadenosine (also called N6-methyladenine or 6mA) was considered to be essentially restricted to the genome of prokaryotes, where this modification plays a well-established role in the restriction-modification system and other processes such as DNA replication or transcription (Sánchez-Romero and Casadesús, 2020; Wion and Casadesús, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by references to prior literature.

claim: 6mA plays a well-established role in the restriction-modification system and other processes such as DNA replication or transcription in prokaryotes.

source: It is thus likely that 6mA levels measured in non-axenic conditions do not solely reflect endogenous 6mA in the Drosophila genome and variations between genotypes should be interpreted with caution.

claim: No significant increase in 6mA levels was observed in the absence of TET in non-axenic conditions in embryos and adult brains.
source: Still, we did not observe any significant increase in 6mA levels in the absence of TET in non-axenic conditions (Figure 1F and G).

claim: No significant increase in 6mA levels was observed in the absence of TET in axenic conditions in embryos and adult brains.
source: Importantly, the same observation was made in axenic conditions (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS measurements shown in Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: The apparent increase in 6mA levels in tetDMAD1/DMAD2 axenic embryos was not reproduced in tetnull embryos.
source: Of note, the apparent increase in 6mA levels in tetDMAD1/DMAD2 axenic embryos was not reproduced in tetnull embryos, suggesting that it does not simply reflect tet loss-of-function, and it was not statistically significant as compared to wild-type levels (Welch two sample t-test: p=0.075).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: The apparent increase in 6mA levels in tetDMAD1/DMAD2 axenic embryos does not simply reflect tet loss-of-function.
source: Of note, the apparent increase in 6mA levels in tetDMAD1/DMAD2 axenic embryos was not reproduced in tetnull embryos, suggesting that it does not simply reflect tet loss-of-function, and it was not statistically significant as compared to wild-type levels (Welch two sample t-test: p=0.075).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of reproducibility in tetnull embryos.

claim: The apparent increase in 6mA levels in tetDMAD1/DMAD2 axenic embryos was not statistically significant as compared to wild-type levels (Welch two sample t-test: p=0.075).
source: Of note, the apparent increase in 6mA levels in tetDMAD1/DMAD2 axenic embryos was not reproduced in tetnull embryos, suggesting that it does not simply reflect tet loss-of-function, and it was not statistically significant as compared to wild-type levels (Welch two sample t-test: p=0.075).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of LC-MS/MS measurements.

claim: No consistent evidence was found that TET loss caused an increase in 6mA levels in embryos, whole larvae, larval CNS, or adult brain.
source: Altogether, we did not find consistent evidence that TET loss caused an increase in 6mA levels in embryos, whole larvae, larval CNS, or adult brain.
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS measurements across multiple tissues and conditions.

claim: SMRT sequencing was used as an alternate method to study TET impact on 6mA.
source: As an alternate method to study TET impact on 6mA, we used SMRT sequencing (Boulias and Greer, 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by the methods described in the manuscript.

claim: SMRT-seq data were generated on CNS gDNA from three biological replicates of wild-type and tetnull larvae.
source: We generated SMRT-seq data on CNS gDNA from three biological replicates of wild-type and tetnull larvae.
evidence: The claim is supported by the methods described in the manuscript.

claim: Around 95% of all the adenines were covered at least 25 x in the merged SMRT-seq datasets.
source: In the resulting fusion datasets, around 95% of all the adenines were covered at least 25 x (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by SMRT-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Using standard parameters (coverage ≥25 x and QV ≥20), 0.158% and 0.172% of potential 6mA were found in the CNS of wild-type and tetnull larvae, respectively.
source: Using standard parameters (coverage ≥25 x and QV ≥20), we found respectively, 0.158% and 0.172% of potential 6mA in the CNS of wild-type and tetnull larvae (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 2), which is much more than expected based on LC-MS/MS measurements.
evidence: The claim is supported by SMRT-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The percentage of potential 6mA found by SMRT-seq is much more than expected based on LC-MS/MS measurements.
source: Using standard parameters (coverage ≥25 x and QV ≥20), we found respectively, 0.158% and 0.172% of potential 6mA in the CNS of wild-type and tetnull larvae (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 2), which is much more than expected based on LC-MS/MS measurements.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing SMRT-seq and LC-MS/MS results.

claim: Only 2.6% of potential 6mA were labeled as 6mA in all three SMRT-seq replicates.
source: However, when we considered the methylation status of these adenines in the individual samples, only 2.6% were labeled as 6mA in all three replicates and 13.7% in at least two replicates (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 3), consistent with the idea that SMRT-seq gives a high rate of false positives in organisms containing low 6mA levels (Douvlataniotis et al., 2020; Kong et al., 2023; Schadt et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by SMRT-seq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 13.7% of potential 6mA were labeled as 6mA in at least two SMRT-seq replicates.
source: However, when we considered the methylation status of these adenines in the individual samples, only 2.6% were labeled as 6mA in all three replicates and 13.7% in at least two replicates (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 3), consistent with the idea that SMRT-seq gives a high rate of false positives in organisms containing low 6mA levels (Douvlataniotis et al., 2020; Kong et al., 2023; Schadt et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by SMRT-seq data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: SMRT-seq gives a high rate of false positives in organisms containing low 6mA levels.
source: However, when we considered the methylation status of these adenines in the individual samples, only 2.6% were labeled as 6mA in all three replicates and 13.7% in at least two replicates (Figure 2B and Supplementary file 3), consistent with the idea that SMRT-seq gives a high rate of false positives in organisms containing low 6mA levels (Douvlataniotis et al., 2020; Kong et al., 2023; Schadt et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature and SMRT-seq data.

claim: Increasing the QV strongly ameliorated the fraction of replication and drastically reduced the proportion of potential 6mA both in wild-type and tetnull datasets.
source: Interestingly, increasing the QV strongly ameliorated the fraction of replication and drastically reduced the proportion of potential 6mA both in wild-type and tetnull datasets, whereas increasing the coverage had little effect (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and 3, and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by SMRT-seq data shown in Figures 2A, 2B, and supplements.

claim: Increasing the coverage had little effect on the fraction of replication and proportion of potential 6mA in SMRT-seq datasets.
source: Interestingly, increasing the QV strongly ameliorated the fraction of replication and drastically reduced the proportion of potential 6mA both in wild-type and tetnull datasets, whereas increasing the coverage had little effect (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and 3, and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by SMRT-seq data shown in Figures 2A, 2B, and supplements.

claim: No significant differences were observed in the percentage of 6mA/A or in the fraction of methylation of potential 6mA between wild-type and tetnull samples even with stringent QV values.
source: However, we did not observe any significant differences either in the percentage of 6mA/A or in the fraction of methylation of these potential 6mA even with stringent QV values (Figure 2C and D and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by SMRT-seq data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: SMRT-seq data are noisy.
source: Hence, while SMRT-seq data are noisy, as cautioned in previous studies, they did not reveal an increase in 6mA levels in the absence of TET.
evidence: The claim is supported by SMRT-seq data and citations to prior literature.

claim: SMRT-seq data did not reveal an increase in 6mA levels in the absence of TET.
source: Hence, while SMRT-seq data are noisy, as cautioned in previous studies, they did not reveal an increase in 6mA levels in the absence of TET.
evidence: The claim is supported by SMRT-seq data.

claim: The recombinant catalytic domain of Drosophila TET was incubated with double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) containing either a 5mC or a 6mA modification to test whether TET demethylates 6mA.
source: To directly test whether TET demethylates 6mA, we then assessed its activity in vitro. Accordingly, the recombinant catalytic domain of Drosophila TET was incubated with double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) containing either a 5mC or a 6mA modification and the level of modified bases was quantified by LC-MS/MS at different time points.
evidence: The claim is supported by the methods described in the manuscript.

claim: 5mC levels were drastically reduced in 1 min with the concomitant appearance of 5mC oxidation products (5hmC and 5fC) in the in vitro TET activity assay.
source: Under our experimental conditions, 5mC levels were drastically reduced in 1 min with the concomitant appearance of 5mC oxidation products (5hmC and 5fC) (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The level of 6mA remained constant even after 30 min of incubation with recombinant TET in vitro.
source: In sharp contrast, the level of 6mA remained constant even after 30 min of incubation (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 6mA does not seem to be a good substrate for Drosophila TET in vitro.
source: Hence, contrary to 5mC, 6mA does not seem to be a good substrate for Drosophila TET in vitro.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the in vitro TET activity assay results.

claim: Only traces of 5mC, 5hmC, 5fC, or 6mA were observed when recombinant TET was incubated with non-modified dsDNA.
source: Of note, only traces of 5mC, 5hmC, 5fC, or 6mA were observed when recombinant TET was incubated with non-modified dsDNA, indicating that the levels measured in the presence of modified dsDNA were not due to contaminations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The levels of modified bases measured in the presence of modified dsDNA were not due to contaminations.
source: Of note, only traces of 5mC, 5hmC, 5fC, or 6mA were observed when recombinant TET was incubated with non-modified dsDNA, indicating that the levels measured in the presence of modified dsDNA were not due to contaminations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the control experiment with non-modified dsDNA.

claim: Previous reports showed that recombinant Drosophila TET demethylates 6mA on dsDNA in vitro.
source: Our results contrast with previous reports showing that recombinant Drosophila TET demethylates 6mA on dsDNA in vitro (Yao et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Previous studies ran much longer reactions (up to 10 hr) and used different sources of recombinant protein (Drosophila TET catalytic domain purified from human HEK293T cells).
source: However, both studies ran much longer reactions (up to 10 hr) and used different sources of recombinant protein (Drosophila TET catalytic domain purified from human HEK293T cells).
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing the current study with prior literature.

claim: Zhang et al., 2015 only found around 2.5% of 6mA demethylation at 30 min and less than 25% after 10 hr of incubation as measured by HPLC-MS/MS analyses.
source: Notably, Zhang et al., 2015 only found around 2.5% of 6mA demethylation at 30 min and less than 25% after 10 hr of incubation as measured by HPLC-MS/MS analyses.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Drosophila TET may oxidize 6mA, but with a much lower affinity than 5mC.
source: These results suggest that Drosophila TET may oxidize 6mA, but with a much lower affinity than 5mC since we observed a near complete oxidation of 5mC after 1 min. and no significant decrease in 6mA levels after 30 min. of reaction (for identical concentrations of substrate and enzyme).
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing the in vitro activity of TET on 5mC versus 6mA.

claim: The preparation of TET catalytic domain in different systems may change its enzymatic activity, potentially in relation to distinct post-translational modifications.
source: It is possible too that the preparation of TET catalytic domain in different systems changes its enzymatic activity, potentially in relation to distinct post-translational modifications.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about possible explanations for differences in results.

claim: A distant TET homolog in the fungus Coprinopsis cinerea was recently shown to oxidize both 5mC and 6mA.
source: Still, it is worth mentioning that a distant TET homolog in the fungus Coprinopsis cinerea was recently shown to oxidize both 5mC and 6mA (Mu et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The capacity of Coprinopsis cinerea TET to bind and demethylate 6mA requires key residues within its catalytic domain which are not conserved in other TET homologs including in Drosophila.
source: Importantly, its peculiar capacity to bind and demethylate 6mA requires key residues within its catalytic domain which are not conserved in other TET homologs including in Drosophila (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The observations support the conclusion that Drosophila TET does not serve as 6mA demethylase.
source: These observations support our conclusion that Drosophila TET does not serve as 6mA demethylase.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the in vitro activity assays and sequence comparisons.

claim: Previous reports suggested that TET controls fly viability, ovarian development, or adult brain formation by demethylating 6mA.
source: Although previous reports suggested that TET controls fly viability, ovarian development, or adult brain formation by demethylating 6mA (Yao et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015), the functional importance of TET enzymatic activity has never been tested genetically as available tet alleles either abolish its expression or delete the whole catalytic domain.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The functional importance of TET enzymatic activity has never been tested genetically as available tet alleles either abolish its expression or delete the whole catalytic domain.
source: Although previous reports suggested that TET controls fly viability, ovarian development, or adult brain formation by demethylating 6mA (Yao et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015), the functional importance of TET enzymatic activity has never been tested genetically as available tet alleles either abolish its expression or delete the whole catalytic domain.
evidence: The claim is supported by knowledge of available tet alleles.

claim: A catalytic dead mutant allele of tet (tetCD) was generated.
source: In view of our results and to address this issue, we generated a catalytic dead mutant allele of tet (tetCD).
evidence: The claim is supported by the methods described in the manuscript.

claim: The conserved HxD iron-binding motif required for the catalytic activity of TET/AlkB dioxygenase family of enzymes was mutated by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated homologous recombination.
source: Accordingly, the conserved HxD iron-binding motif required for the catalytic activity of TET/AlkB dioxygenase family of enzymes (Hu et al., 2013; Tahiliani et al., 2009; Xu and Bochtler, 2020) was mutated by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated homologous recombination using a tet-GFP knock-in which allows to tag all protein TET isoforms with GFP (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the methods described in the manuscript and shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Immunostaining in the larval CNS confirmed that TET is widely expressed in this tissue.
source: Of note, immunostaining in the larval CNS confirmed that TET is widely expressed in this tissue and showed that the H1947Y/D1949A mutation does not alter TET expression or its nuclear localization (Figure 4C–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 4C–H.

claim: The H1947Y/D1949A mutation does not alter TET expression or its nuclear localization.
source: Of note, immunostaining in the larval CNS confirmed that TET is widely expressed in this tissue and showed that the H1947Y/D1949A mutation does not alter TET expression or its nuclear localization (Figure 4C–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 4C–H.

claim: tetnull homozygote individuals die at the pupal stage.
source: Strikingly, while tetnull homozygote individuals die at the pupal stage (Delatte et al., 2016), we found that tetCD/CD as well as tetCD/null pupae had a normal hatching rate and gave rise to viable adult flies (Figure 4I).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: tetCD/CD as well as tetCD/null pupae had a normal hatching rate and gave rise to viable adult flies.
source: Strikingly, while tetnull homozygote individuals die at the pupal stage (Delatte et al., 2016), we found that tetCD/CD as well as tetCD/null pupae had a normal hatching rate and gave rise to viable adult flies (Figure 4I).
evidence: The claim is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Lethality of tetCD/CD individuals was not observed at earlier developmental stages.
source: We did not observe the lethality of tetCD/CD individuals at earlier developmental stages either (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: tetCD/CD flies did not exhibit the 'held out' wing positioning defects present in tetDMAD1/DMAD2 adult escapers.
source: Yet, tetCD/CD flies did not exhibit the 'held out' wing positioning defects present in tetDMAD1/DMAD2 adult escapers (Figure 4J, J' and J'').
evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic analysis shown in Figures 4J, J', and J''.

claim: Atrophied ovaries or mushroom body projection defects observed in the absence of TET expression were not reproduced when only its catalytic activity was impaired.
source: Similarly, atrophied ovaries or mushroom body projection defects observed in the absence of TET expression were not reproduced when only its catalytic activity was impaired (Figure 4K, K', K" , L and L', L'').
evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic analysis shown in Figures 4K, K', K'', L, L', and L''.

claim: TET function in Drosophila seems essentially independent of its enzymatic activity.
source: Thus, TET function in Drosophila seems essentially independent of its enzymatic activity, indicating that TET-mediated regulation of 6mA level, if it truly happens, is not essential either for fly development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the viability and phenotypic analysis of catalytic-dead TET mutants.

claim: TET-mediated regulation of 6mA level, if it truly happens, is not essential for fly development.
source: Thus, TET function in Drosophila seems essentially independent of its enzymatic activity, indicating that TET-mediated regulation of 6mA level, if it truly happens, is not essential either for fly development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the viability and phenotypic analysis of catalytic-dead TET mutants.

claim: 6mA is unlikely to play a major regulatory function in normal conditions in Drosophila.
source: In sum, our results confirm that 6mA is present only at very low levels in the Drosophila genome. With only a few hundred methylated adenines per haplogenome, we argue that 6mA is unlikely to play a major regulatory function in normal conditions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the very low 6mA levels measured.

claim: TET is not a methyladenine demethylase.
source: In addition, we did not find any evidence that TET loss promotes 6mA accumulation. Rather, our results strongly suggest that this conserved enzyme is not a methyladenine demethylase and that its catalytic activity is largely dispensable for Drosophila development.
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS, SMRT-seq, and in vitro activity assay data.

claim: TET catalytic activity is largely dispensable for Drosophila development.
source: In addition, we did not find any evidence that TET loss promotes 6mA accumulation. Rather, our results strongly suggest that this conserved enzyme is not a methyladenine demethylase and that its catalytic activity is largely dispensable for Drosophila development.
evidence: The claim is supported by viability and phenotypic analysis of catalytic-dead TET mutants.

claim: Further experiments will be necessary to firmly establish whether regulated adenine methylation/demethylation takes place and what are the enzymes involved, not only in Drosophila but also in other metazoans.
source: Further experiments will be necessary to firmly establish whether regulated adenine methylation/demethylation takes place and what are the enzymes involved, not only in Drosophila but also in other metazoans.
evidence: The claim is a statement about future research needs.

claim: The analyses call for further investigations of the molecular mechanisms underlying the essential, enzymatic-independent, mode of action of TET.
